sections.text: This army of ours marshalled by Bhishma is insufficient, whereas that army of theirs marshalled by Bhima is sufficient.
Therefore do ye all, stationed in your respective positions, in the several divisions of the army, protect Bhishma alone.
His glorious grandsire (Bhishma), the oldest of the Kauravas, in order to cheer Duryodhana, now roared like a lion, and blew his conch.

Now we come to a very important verse, verse 10. After all that enumeration of warriors on both sides, Duryodhana finally gives his conclusion. Aparyaptam tad asmakam balam Bhishma abhiraksitam, paryaptam tvidam etesham balam Bhima abhiraksitam.
This verse has puzzled commentators for centuries because the word Aparyaptam can mean two completely opposite things. One meaning is unlimited, immeasurable, plenty. The other meaning is insufficient, not enough. So the same verse can be read two ways.
First reading: Our army protected by Bhishma is unlimited, immeasurable. Their army protected by Bhima is limited, measurable. We have more, they have less. We are going to win.
Second reading: Our army protected by Bhishma is insufficient. Their army protected by Bhima is sufficient. Despite having more soldiers, we may not have enough.
Now, which interpretation is correct? I think both are correct, and thats exactly the point. This is what anxiety does to the mind. One moment you feel confident: I have eleven akshauhinis, they have only seven, how can I lose? The next moment doubt creeps in: But look at their warriors, Arjuna, Bhima, Drishtadyumna. What if its not enough?
We see this in our own lives, dont we? Before a big presentation, one moment you think Ive prepared well, I know this material, Ill do great. The next moment: But what if they ask something I dont know? What if the competition is better? This oscillation between confidence and doubt, this is the Duryodhana mind at work.
Notice something interesting here. Duryodhana says the Pandava army is protected by Bhima. But Bhima was not the commander, Dhrishtadyumna was the commander of the Pandava forces. So why does Duryodhana name Bhima instead of the actual commander?
The simple answer is that Bhima was Duryodhanas direct rival. Both were mace warriors. From childhood, they competed with each other. Duryodhana knew that if this war came down to a final confrontation, it would be between him and Bhima. So in his mind, Bhima was the one who mattered, not the official commander.
This is how our mind works. The person who keeps us up at night is not always the official competitor, the one on paper. Its the one we measure ourselves against. In the office, it may not be your actual boss who creates anxiety, its that one colleague who seems to be doing everything better than you.
Now verse 11: Ayanesu cha sarveshu yathabhagam avasthitah, Bhishmam eva abhirakshantu bhavantah sarva eva hi.
Duryodhana gives his first tactical command: All of you, stationed in your respective positions at the various entry points, must protect Bhishma alone. Protect Bhishma at all costs.
Think about this. You are about to fight the most important battle of your life. What is your first command to your troops? Is it Attack! or Charge forward! or Victory will be ours!? No. Duryodhanas first command is defensive, protect our most valuable asset.
This reveals his mindset completely. He knows that Bhishma is the pillar of his army. If Bhishma falls, everything falls. So instead of inspiring his troops with an offensive vision, his first instinct is defensive. Cover our weakness. Protect what we have.
We do this too. When we are insecure about something, our first instinct is to protect rather than to advance. A person insecure about their job starts hoarding information instead of sharing it. A person insecure in a relationship starts becoming possessive instead of nurturing. Defense becomes the primary mode of operation.
Now comes verse 12, and the whole energy shifts. Sanjaya narrates: Tasya sanjanayan harsham kuruvriddhah pitamahah, simhanadam vinadyoccaih shankham dadhmau pratapavan.
To cheer up Duryodhana, the mighty grandsire of the Kurus, Bhishma, roared like a lion and blew his conch loudly.
Look at what is happening here. Bhishma has been watching this whole scene. He sees his grandson going to Drona, nervously listing warriors, questioning loyalties, giving defensive commands. He sees the anxiety spreading through the ranks like a contagion. And he decides enough is enough.
Bhishma doesnt give a speech. He doesnt offer reassurance. He doesnt say Dont worry, we will win. He simply roars like a lion and blows his conch.
This is leadership. When the team is spiraling into anxiety, sometimes the best thing a leader can do is not engage with the anxiety but cut through it with decisive action. The lions roar says: We are warriors. This is what we do. Lets begin.
I remember once being in a meeting where everyone was going around in circles, worried about all the things that could go wrong with a project. The more we discussed, the more anxious everyone became. Finally, the senior partner stood up and said, Weve talked enough. Lets start. And he walked out to begin work. That was his lions roar.
The conch is significant too. In those days, the blowing of conches formally signaled the beginning of battle. It was like the opening bell of a boxing match. Once the conch sounds, theres no more time for deliberation. You fight.
By blowing his conch first, Bhishma is taking charge. Hes saying: I may be bound by my vow to serve whoever sits on the throne of Hastinapura, even if its Duryodhana. But I am still the grandsire. I am still the commander. And I say its time to begin.
Theres something else worth noting. The verse says Bhishma did this tasya sanjanayan harsham, to generate joy, to cheer up Duryodhana. Bhishma saw that his grandson was collapsing under the weight of his own anxiety. And even though Bhishma personally knew that the Kaurava cause was not righteous, even though he had tried multiple times to prevent this war, once committed, he gave his complete presence.
This is the dharma of a warrior. Once you have made your decision, stop second-guessing. Bhishmas conch blast was his way of saying: The time for doubt is over. Now we act.
What a contrast between these two, Duryodhana and Bhishma. Both on the same side. Both fighting for the same cause. Yet one is consumed by anxiety despite having more resources, while the other is calm and decisive despite knowing the cause is flawed.
This tells us something important: our inner state is not determined by our external circumstances or even by whether our cause is just. Its determined by our relationship with our own mind. Duryodhana, fighting for what he believed was rightfully his to keep, could not find peace. Bhishma, fighting for a cause he knew was wrong, found a way to be at peace with his situation.
How? Bhishma had accepted. He had accepted his vow, accepted his circumstances, accepted that he could not control the outcome. This acceptance gave him a stability that Duryodhana, constantly grasping and fearing loss, could never access.
As we move forward in the Gita, we will see more of this theme. Krishna will teach Arjuna that peace comes not from controlling outcomes but from doing ones duty with detachment. Bhishma, in his own way, had already learned this lesson.
With Bhishmas conch blast, the Kurukshetra war officially begins. From this moment, there is no turning back. Every character we have met, Dhritarashtra in his palace, Duryodhana in his anxiety, Drona with his divided loyalties, all of them are now locked into the great wheel of karma that will turn for eighteen days.
And somewhere in the middle of the battlefield, Krishna and Arjuna sit in their chariot, about to have the conversation that will change everything.

Verse 10 contains an intriguing ambiguity: Aparyaptam can mean either unlimited (our army is so vast) or insufficient (our army is not enough). This wordplay captures Duryodhanas conflicted mind perfectly, he oscillates between arrogance and anxiety. Notice how he compares armies by their protectors: his side guarded by Bhishma, the Pandavas by Bhima. Interestingly, he names Bhima rather than the actual commander Dhrishtadyumna, revealing that his real rival, the one who haunts his thoughts, is Bhima, his equal in mace warfare.
Then comes Bhishmas response in verse 12: seeing Duryodhanas nervous energy spreading to the troops, the grandsire roared like a lion and blew his conch to cheer them up. This is true leadership, recognizing when anxiety is contagious and acting decisively to shift the energy. Bhishma doesnt engage with Duryodhanas insecurity; he simply signals that its time to begin.
Reflect on situations where youve been like Duryodhana, simultaneously boasting about your resources while secretly doubting their sufficiency. Notice how this anxiety affects those around you. Then consider: who are the Bhishmas in your life, the wise elders who cut through uncertainty with decisive action? And when might you need to be that person for others? Sometimes the most helpful response to collective anxiety isnt more analysis or reassurance, but a clear signal that its time to move forward. What conch might you need to blow in your own life to shift from deliberation to action?
